entry.title: [loofah] Loofah: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses
entry.content:
Summary

Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a :url or :bad_url, and left url out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the style attribute. When scrub_css rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — url\28 …\29 — hid the url token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into a live url() that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

Impact

A sanitized style attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to an attacker-chosen URL. list-style fetches on render with no interaction, cursor on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist and display it to other people are affected.

Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

References

  • https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-m3x9-938q-5767
  • https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/pull/324

entry.title: [loofah] Loofah: Regular expression denial of service in the SVG local-reference check
entry.content:
Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the href and xlink:href attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against /^\s*[^#\s].*/m. In Ruby ^ anchors to every line start and \s matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose href or xlink:href is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF, so no configuration change is required.

Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3. Applications that cannot upgrade should run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.

Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

References

  • https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-mf2j-8f84-cc9q
  • https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/pull/324

entry.title: [loofah] Loofah allowed_uri? treats data:text/html as safe text/plain
entry.content:
Summary

Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? returns true for a data: URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference / in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed text/plain, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as text/html.

Details

allowed_uri? decodes HTML entities with CGI.unescapeHTML, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. / therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no /, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed text/plain under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

:, /, 	 and 
 are the only named character references in the HTML5 table that decode to characters that change how a URI parses (U+003A, U+002F, U+0009 and U+000A; there is no named reference for U+000D), so this closes the set.

Loofah's default sanitize() path is not affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public allowed_uri? string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? and then render the approved value into an href or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri? re-exports the same helper.

Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @ngpestelos.

References

entry.title: [loofah] Loofah: Mutation XSS in the HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
entry.content:
Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape < and > in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The :strip scrubber is affected in every browser. The :prune and :escape scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes < and > in attribute values, as the HTML standard requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API (Loofah.html5_fragment, Loofah.html5_document and the scrub_html5_* methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with the default allowlist.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including Loofah::Helpers.sanitize), the :whitewash scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and JRuby.

Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

References

entry.title: [activestorage] Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file read and remote code execution in video previews, analysis and image processing
entry.content:
Impact

ActiveStorage::Blob#open writes a blob to a tempfile whose name carries the extension of the uploaded filename, and hands that path to ffprobe (VideoAnalyzer, AudioAnalyzer), ffmpeg (VideoPreviewer) and ImageMagick (ImageAnalyzer, the :mini_magick variant processor). These tools select a decoder from the file extension when the content does not identify its own format, so an attacker who chooses the filename and declares the content type of an upload chooses which decoder processes it. An FFmpeg built with AviSynth support treats a file with the .avs extension as an AviSynth script and evaluates it, which could disclose files readable by the application process through the preview image, or load a native library the attacker has also uploaded, possibly leading to remote code execution in the FFmpeg process. ImageMagick selects its coders and delegates from the extension in the same way.

Details

The fixed releases keep the uploaded extension on the tempfile only when Marcel maps that extension to the blob's recorded content type, and name the tempfile with no extension otherwise. A form upload whose Rack tempfile fails the same check is copied to a correctly named tempfile before processing. Files whose uploaded extension disagrees with their content type are still processed; the external tool detects their format from the content. The Active Storage CHANGELOG describes the change.

Affected applications

An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:

  • Accepts uploads from untrusted users.
  • Analyzes video or audio attachments (which Active Storage does on attach by default), generates video previews, or processes images with ImageMagick.

The AviSynth attack additionally requires an FFmpeg built with --enable-avisynth and the AviSynthPlus runtime on the host. Upstream FFmpeg and the common Linux distribution and Homebrew packages do not enable it; the GPL builds distributed for Windows and Linux from ffmpeg.org do. Other decoders that FFmpeg or ImageMagick select from the extension may be reachable without AviSynth.

Mitigation

  • Upgrade to a fixed version of activestorage.

Expire and change secrets

Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not undo a disclosure that already occurred. An application that meets the AviSynth requirement above should treat every secret readable by the application process as potentially exposed and change it, including secret_key_base, the master key and everything in config/credentials.yml.enc that it decrypts, the Active Storage service credentials, database credentials, and tokens for third-party services. Changing secret_key_base expires active sessions and invalidates signed and encrypted cookies, signed global IDs and Active Storage URLs. Do not retain an exposed secret as a fallback.

Workarounds

Applications that cannot upgrade can stop Active Storage from running FFmpeg on uploaded files by removing ActiveStorage::Previewer::VideoPreviewer from config.active_storage.previewers, and ActiveStorage::Analyzer::VideoAnalyzer and ActiveStorage::Analyzer::AudioAnalyzer from config.active_storage.analyzers. Running an FFmpeg built without AviSynth support closes the AviSynth attack but not the extension-selected decoders of ImageMagick.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/72136ff39153bc8d63ecbc899993848eb3d6573e.patch
  • 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8106938fb0a595f11006dd1497cd409e27d7d636.patch

Versions affected

  • activestorage < 8.0.5.2
  • activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher pirikara.

References

  • https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh

entry.title: [activestorage] Active Storage: Possible circumvention of file size limits in Active Storage direct uploads to Google Cloud Storage
entry.content:
Impact

ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload does not bind the declared content length into the signed direct-upload URL, and #headers_for_direct_upload returns no length constraint, so the URL authorizes an upload body of any size. A direct-upload client could store a file larger than the byte_size it declared, and the resulting blob keeps the declared size, possibly bypassing application file size validations and quotas. This is the weakness that CVE-2020-8162 fixed in the S3 service.

Applications that store files in Google Cloud Storage and accept direct uploads are affected.

Details

The fixed releases sign an x-goog-content-length-range header that matches the blob's declared byte_size and return it from headers_for_direct_upload, so Cloud Storage rejects an upload body of any other size. Browsers send this header with the direct upload, so a bucket's CORS configuration must list x-goog-content-length-range in responseHeader, or browser direct uploads fail after the upgrade. The Active Storage CHANGELOG and the CORS example in the Active Storage guide show the change.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e19916cea31cbfb0030b165ae853b741f8dd57a7.patch
  • 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7fe85a72a789eae5ee070ce3ee1dad10a8a5f70c.patch

Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher f4cts.

entry.title: [activesupport] Active Support: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize
entry.content:
Impact

When constant lookup raises LoadError, ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize (and String#safe_constantize) builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application unavailable.

Action Cable passes the channel value of each subscribe command to safe_constantize before any channel lookup, so in the default configuration an unauthenticated client of the Action Cable endpoint can reach this code.

Details

The check that decides whether safe_constantize returns nil or re-raises the LoadError now matches the first segment of the constant name against the error message as a literal string, and no longer compiles a regular expression. It returns the same result as before for constant names that contain no regular expression syntax.

Affected applications

An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:

  • Mounts Action Cable, which a new Rails application does by default at /cable (config.action_cable.mount_path), or otherwise passes untrusted input to safe_constantize.
  • Accepts Action Cable connections from untrusted clients. ApplicationCable::Connection#connect authenticates nobody unless the application adds a check.

Workarounds

Applications that do not use Action Cable can set config.action_cable.mount_path = nil to remove the endpoint. Applications that use Action Cable can call reject_unauthorized_connection in ApplicationCable::Connection#connect for unauthenticated clients, which limits exposure to authenticated users but does not remove it.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/95aa9e416016524956d4904fed96eaed079580bb.patch
  • 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/210ac22d446c8e2625b091e79256806b836eee20.patch

Versions affected

  • activesupport < 8.0.5.2
  • activesupport >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Felix Tscheulin (flixt) through HackerOne researcher scheja, and independently by Bucky Wolfe (Igneous), who provided a proof of concept that crashes the server. It was also found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-ZUN5KU3Q).

entry.title: [activestorage] Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage filename handling
entry.content:
Impact

ActiveStorage::Filename#base and #extension_with_delimiter, and therefore #extension, pass the stored filename unmodified to File.basename and File.extname, which raise ArgumentError when the name contains a NUL byte. Active Storage stores the client-supplied filename verbatim, so a user who is permitted to upload an attachment could persist such a filename on databases that accept NUL bytes in string columns, such as SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB. Each subsequent request that builds a variant or preview of the blob, opens it, or renders it as an Action Text attachment then raises, possibly resulting in a persistent DoS vulnerability for the pages that display the blob until it is purged or its filename is corrected. Applications that use PostgreSQL are not affected, because PostgreSQL rejects the row.

Details

Filename#base and #extension_with_delimiter now derive from Filename#sanitized, the form that Filename#to_s and the Content-Disposition header already use. entry.title: [activestorage] Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage filename handling
entry.content:
Impact

ActiveStorage::Filename#base and #extension_with_delimiter, and therefore #extension, pass the stored filename unmodified to File.basename and File.extname, which raise ArgumentError when the name contains a NUL byte. Active Storage stores the client-supplied filename verbatim, so a user who is permitted to upload an attachment could persist such a filename on databases that accept NUL bytes in string columns, such as SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB. Each subsequent request that builds a variant or preview of the blob, opens it, or renders it as an Action Text attachment then raises, possibly resulting in a persistent DoS vulnerability for the pages that display the blob until it is purged or its filename is corrected. Applications that use PostgreSQL are not affected, because PostgreSQL rejects the row.

Filename#base and #extension_with_delimiter now derive from Filename#sanitized, the form that Filename#to_s and the Content-Disposition header already use. entry.title: [actionmailbox] Action Mailbox: Possible signature replay in Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress
entry.content:
Impact

The Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress authenticates a request with an HMAC of the timestamp and token parameters concatenated without a separator, and ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::InboundEmailsController::Authenticator#recent? rejects only timestamps more than 2 minutes in the past. Because the signature does not fix the boundary between the two values, a captured signed request can be presented with a timestamp far in the future, which the ingress then accepts indefinitely. An attacker who obtains one signed Mailgun webhook request, but not the signing key, could submit arbitrary inbound email that Action Mailbox processes as genuine, possibly leading to forged messages attributed to the sender of the attacker's choosing.

Applications that receive inbound email through the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress are affected.

Details

The fixed releases also reject a Mailgun request whose timestamp is more than 2 minutes ahead of the server's clock, as they already did for one more than 2 minutes behind it. An application whose clock runs more than 2 minutes behind Mailgun's will now reject genuine webhooks and should synchronize its clock.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c3a295c5c22266e8ec4d0e664e6923a299235e7a.patch

entry.title: [activesupport] Active Support: Possible XSS vulnerability in Active Support MessagePack serializer
entry.content:
Impact

ActiveSupport::MessagePack serializes an ActiveSupport::SafeBuffer as its bytes alone and deserializes it as a new SafeBuffer, so a buffer that is no longer html_safe? (for example, one mutated in place with gsub!) is restored as html_safe. If such a buffer holds untrusted input and is stored through a MessagePack serializer, rendering it after it is loaded bypasses ERB auto-escaping, possibly leading to XSS.

Applications on Rails 8.1 are affected if they use a MessagePack serializer, such as config.action_dispatch.cookies_serializer = :message_pack or :message_pack_allow_marshal, or serializer: :message_pack for Rails.cache, ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier or ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor, and store a SafeBuffer that was mutated in place with untrusted input. Rails 8.0 and earlier do not serialize SafeBuffer with MessagePack and are not affected.

Details

The fixed releases serialize a SafeBuffer that is not html_safe? with a marker and deserialize it as a String; a SafeBuffer that is html_safe? keeps the existing format. Versions without the fix cannot read an unsafe buffer serialized by the fixed releases, so during a rolling deploy a cookie or cache entry holding one could fail to load on a process that has not been upgraded.

Workarounds

Applications that cannot upgrade can convert a SafeBuffer to a String with to_str before storing it in a value that a MessagePack serializer writes.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/4ca090665976e6fbc471c38689b399f84b43cdc7.patch

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher jcwilk.

entry.title: [actionpack] Action Pack: Possible cache poisoning in Action Pack content negotiation
entry.content:
Impact

Action Pack negotiates the format of a rendered response from the Accept, X-Requested-With and, for XHR requests without Accept, Content-Type request headers, but ActionController::Rendering#_set_vary_header adds Vary: Accept only when the request carries a usable Accept header and the response has no Vary header yet. A response to a request without Accept, or to an XHR request, therefore omits the headers that selected its representation, and a response whose Vary the application set before rendering (for example Vary: Accept-Language) never gains Accept. A shared cache that honours Vary could store such a response and serve it to later clients that request a different representation, possibly leading to cache poisoning in which visitors receive, until the entry expires, a page without its layout or HTML in place of JSON. The attacker cannot choose the content of the response.

Applications that render negotiated responses from actions marked public (for example with expires_in ..., public: true) behind a shared cache that honours Vary, such as Thruster or Rack::Cache, are affected.

Details

In the fixed releases, a rendered response whose format is not given by the URL lists Accept and X-Requested-With in Vary, and also Content-Type for an XHR request without Accept; when config.action_dispatch.ignore_accept_header is enabled, it lists only X-Requested-With. These fields are appended to an existing Vary value rather than skipped, and Vary: * is left unchanged. Shared caches can store more variants of such responses than before. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG for details.

Workarounds

Set Vary: Accept, X-Requested-With on negotiated responses in the application, for example in an after_action, or do not mark negotiated responses public.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7a955ca36779938267c93902c47d1f55bab99b4b.patch
  • 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/b58c107abe9c1f10c1d6a4941402c60e4dc4742c.patch

Credit

This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-7GHGLQGO, ANT-2026-5MT6C2R3).

entry.title: [actionpack] Action Pack: Missing SameSite attribute on session cookies from Action Pack session stores
entry.content:
Impact

Action Pack session stores other than ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore (CacheStore, MemCacheStore, and third-party stores built on AbstractStore, AbstractSecureStore or the session mixins) write the session cookie without a SameSite attribute, regardless of config.action_dispatch.cookies_same_site_protection, which defaults to :lax. Only CookieStore applies the configured policy. In browsers that do not treat a cookie without the attribute as SameSite=Lax, a cross-site request could carry the session cookie, possibly leading to cross-site request forgery against actions that do not verify an authenticity token, such as those of API-only applications.

Applications are affected when they use a session store other than CookieStore and do not pass same_site: to config.session_store.

Details

In the fixed releases, every session store sets the session cookie's SameSite attribute from cookies_same_site_protection when its options have no :same_site key. An explicit same_site: option, including same_site: nil, and a :same_site value in a store's DEFAULT_OPTIONS still take precedence.

Workarounds

Pass same_site: when configuring the session store, for example config.session_store :cache_store, same_site: :lax.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

entry.title: [activestorage] Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage proxy mode via storage errors during streaming
entry.content:
Impact

When Active Storage serves a file through its proxy controllers, ActiveStorage::Streaming#send_blob_stream handles an error from the storage service by calling head to send a 404 or 500 response. If the error occurs after the first chunk has been written, the response is already committed, and head replaces the response body while the server is still reading the original ActionController::Live buffer. That buffer is never closed, so the server thread handling the request blocks until the process restarts. Repeated failed downloads could exhaust the server's threads, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability.

Applications are affected when they store files on a service that streams a download in several requests, such as Amazon S3, an S3-compatible service or Google Cloud Storage, and draw Active Storage's default routes. The proxy routes are drawn whether or not proxy mode is the default for the application. A file deleted while it is being served, or any other storage error partway through a download, triggers the condition.

Details

A storage error raised before the response is committed still produces a 404 or 500 response. After the fix, a storage error raised after the response is committed is re-raised instead, so the server closes the streamed response and releases the thread; the client receives a truncated body, and the exception reaches the application's error reporting.

Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

  • 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/3c67a693fb21870ecb1222e3da59d5c491a62009.patch
